title: A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a sustained industrial fuel cycle that repeatedly recovers actinides from used nuclear fuel, makes recovered material into new fuel or irradiation targets, and returns it to reactors for further irradiation and fission. Success would require consuming a substantial, explicitly defined fraction of long-lived actinides across repeated cycles while managing all remaining material and waste. The IAEA describes multiple reprocessing and recycling as a development goal and identifies minor-actinide recycling as a route to reducing the burden of high-level waste.

The central advance would integrate separations, fuel fabrication, irradiation, material accounting and waste conditioning into reliable operation at meaningful throughput. It would extend demonstrated plutonium recycling to sustained recycling that includes minor actinides. Recovering material is one step toward this objective. Establishing consumption requires measuring its subsequent transformation and net destruction across the complete cycle.

Synthesis of the proposed scope. The system could comprise coordinated facilities with different functions. Its performance would be assessed across their combined boundaries, including transfers, inventories, process losses and final waste streams. The phrase “consumes most” remains an intended outcome whose isotope coverage, accounting basis and required fraction must be specified.

significance.text: Successful repeated recycling could substantially improve fuel utilization and reduce the long-lived actinide inventory sent for disposal. The IAEA identifies lower radiotoxicity, lower decay heat and a reduced repository footprint among the intended benefits of minor-actinide recycling. Delivering these benefits at industrial scale would change how much energy and residual disposal burden arise from a given fuel resource. The supplied evidence establishes these qualitative goals without quantifying an achievable destruction fraction, resource multiplier or repository reduction.

Greater uranium utilization would depend on suitable reactor and fuel-cycle pathways, including the ability to convert recovered material into forms that contribute to energy production. Recovery alone does not establish the additional usable energy. The IAEA's broad characterization of fully closed cycles as potentially making nuclear energy nearly renewable expresses the prospective resource benefit. Finite resources, processing losses, infrastructure and operating requirements would still bound practical performance.

Commercial adoption would additionally depend on acceptable economics, safety, safeguards and reliability. The IAEA describes increasing recycling complexity and cost alongside its potential benefits. Reduced waste heat and radiotoxicity could conditionally ease some disposal requirements, but the report continues to recognize waste-management and disposal responsibilities.

Technical inference retained from the research and review. Fission products, unrecovered actinides, process residues and contaminated equipment would continue to require management. Some residual radionuclides could impose long-duration disposal requirements even after efficient actinide destruction. The supplied reviewed passages do not inventory these streams or specifically establish the contribution of long-lived fission products, so their quantities and consequences remain unquantified here. Eliminating radioactive waste or the need for repositories would exceed the demonstrated implications.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability is sustained, integrated recycling with substantial net actinide destruction and acceptable practical performance. In August 2025, the IAEA described mature plutonium recycling, advanced recycling approaching full-scale demonstration, and continuing research on minor-actinide partitioning and transmutation. This establishes a development gap at the report's date. The supplied record does not establish whether a system satisfying every proposed requirement remained undemonstrated through November 2026.

Engineering synthesis of the integration barriers. Separations must recover the intended actinides with sufficiently low cumulative losses over repeated passes. Fabrication must turn the recovered mixtures into usable fuels or targets, and irradiation must achieve the intended net destruction while preserving reliable reactor operation. Material compositions and inventories change through processing and irradiation, so successful operation must remain repeatable as recycled material evolves. Individual successful steps leave the combined throughput, losses and reliability to be demonstrated.

Engineering synthesis of the practical barriers. Facilities must handle radioactive materials while controlling worker exposure, public exposure and environmental releases. Material accounting and safeguards must remain credible across processing, fabrication, irradiation, storage and transfers. Waste conditioning must accommodate every resulting stream. Together, these requirements must yield lifecycle costs and operating availability compatible with deployment. The supplied evidence provides no integrated measurements establishing that all these conditions have been met.

current_state.text: The IAEA Director General's International Status and Prospects for Nuclear Power 2025, dated 25 August 2025, documents operational antecedents. Paragraph 85 reports that Russia's commercial BN-800 fast reactor was fully loaded with mixed-oxide fuel containing plutonium recovered from spent nuclear fuel. This supports a specific achievement in recovered-plutonium fuel use. It supplies no demonstration of repeated minor-actinide recycling or the complete system's net destruction, process losses, economics and safeguards performance.

The surrounding discussion describes mature plutonium recycling and advanced recycling approaching full-scale demonstration. Paragraph 80 identifies minor-actinide partitioning and transmutation as continuing research intended to reduce high-level waste heat generation and radiotoxicity. Paragraphs 81–84 discuss resource utilization and more complete recycling. These statements establish a mixture of operating capabilities and development objectives as of August 2025. They leave the proposed integrated, multi-recycle performance unproven in the supplied record.

The supplied review verified the IAEA report's identity from its internal bibliographic information. It located the relevant discussion on PDF page 24, printed page 20, with disposal responsibilities addressed in later paragraphs. The retained extraction was not marked truncated, but some PDF pages lacked extractable text, preventing confirmation of overall completeness. The reviewed passages support the dated findings above. The empty supplied bounded-search record leaves subsequent developments through 1 November 2026, and the position at the 11 November 2026 retrieval date, unresolved.

The retained ARPA-E page contains a readable headline announcing $40 million for an approach to reducing the impact of used nuclear fuel, together with navigation text. Its substantive announcement body, date and NEWTON identification were absent from the retained material. Consequently, the supplied review could not independently assess the program's identity, funding details, technical scope or achievements. The source index's NEWTON label remains insufficient to resolve those questions.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Integrated or coordinated facilities would repeatedly process representative commercial spent fuel, fabricate recovered materials into fuels or targets, and irradiate them through multiple cycles. The campaign would cover clearly specified feed compositions and operating conditions. Independent accounting would follow nuclear material through every facility, transfer, inventory and waste stream. These proposed criteria translate the recycling objective into an assessable program.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatedly recycle commercial spent fuel through multiple irradiation cycles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting requirements. Publish isotope-resolved initial and final inventories, recovery fractions, process losses and net actinide destruction, accounting for actinides produced during irradiation as well as those consumed. Report measurement uncertainty and material balances. Before the campaign, define the isotope set, denominator, time horizon and required fraction associated with “most long-lived actinides.” Recovered material awaiting irradiation and material transferred to another facility would remain visible in the accounting.
completion_criteria.label: Isotope-resolved accounting quantifies net destruction against predefined “most” criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical acceptance requirements. Establish quantitative thresholds and a comparison baseline before demonstration for lifecycle cost, worker and public exposure, environmental releases, operating reliability, safeguards performance and residual disposal needs. Define throughput relative to the spent-fuel generation or accumulated inventory the system is intended to address. Publish the resulting waste quantities, compositions, heat burdens and disposal requirements alongside actinide-consumption results. The supplied evidence establishes no accepted numerical thresholds for these measures.
completion_criteria.label: Report practical performance against predefined thresholds and comparison baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements. Repeated campaigns, independent verification and sufficiently transparent methods and results would establish whether performance persists across cycles and representative feed variations. Report the fuel types, facilities, reactor conditions, maintenance demands and operating limits actually demonstrated. Finite campaigns would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, leaving broader applicability to further testing.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated campaigns independently verify performance within reported operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. NUC-02, “Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost,” shares the requirement for commercially deployable nuclear infrastructure. Lower plant costs could improve the economics of reactors participating in a closed cycle, while NUC-03 separately requires economical separations, fabrication, repeated irradiation and waste handling. NUC-10, “Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites,” concerns dependable service with infrequent intervention. Its connection to NUC-03 would depend on arrangements for fuel return, transport and centralized recycling.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-06, “Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure,” and NUC-11, “Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants,” address enabling materials and operating-lifetime constraints that could affect selected recycling reactors. NUC-09, “Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention,” addresses fuel endurance and retention during irradiation. NUC-03 extends across repeated recovery, refabrication and irradiation, requiring performance beyond a single fuel residence.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-05, “Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors,” could contribute information about reactor activity relevant to oversight. NUC-12, “Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis,” could support monitoring of irradiation conditions and core behavior. NUC-13, “A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance,” overlaps directly with the handling and accounting of recovered nuclear materials. Each would address a distinct requirement within or alongside a closed fuel cycle, whose complete material balance would still need verification.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-08, “Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling,” concerns safety functions relevant to participating reactors. Its success would address part of the operational safety case, while separations, fabrication, material transport and waste facilities would retain their own performance requirements.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-01, “A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant,” and NUC-07, “Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle,” pursue different energy-production breakthroughs. Any contribution from fusion-derived neutrons to actinide processing would require a separately demonstrated coupling, which the supplied record does not establish. NUC-04, “High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions,” concerns propulsion performance and mission operations. A connection through fuel supply or eventual fuel recovery would depend on a specific system design.

unresolved_issues: Whether an integrated system meeting all proposed requirements had been demonstrated after August 2025 remains unresolved in the supplied record.
The isotope coverage, accounting basis, required consumption fraction, acceptance thresholds and meaningful throughput for this innovation remain undefined.
Integrated measurements of net destruction, cumulative losses, lifecycle economics, exposures, releases, safeguards performance and operating reliability are absent from the supplied evidence.
The quantities and disposal implications of residual fission products, process residues, unrecovered actinides and contaminated equipment remain unquantified.
The retained ARPA-E artifact does not establish the announcement date, NEWTON identity, substantive program details or demonstrated outcomes.
Some IAEA PDF pages lacked extractable text, leaving overall retained-document completeness unconfirmed despite usable reviewed passages.

brief.title: Repeated nuclear fuel recycling with less lasting waste
possible: Nuclear power operators could reuse spent fuel repeatedly, consuming most of its long-lived actinides, a family of radioactive elements. Recovered material would become fresh fuel or material placed in reactors to be transformed and consumed.
why: Repeated recycling could extract more energy from nuclear fuel and leave fewer long-lived actinides for disposal. For communities managing nuclear waste, that could mean less heat, less harm from radiation and less space needed underground.

sources.showed: The agency reports that Russia’s commercial BN-800 reactor was fully loaded with fuel containing recovered plutonium. It describes recycling other actinides as continuing research.
sources.cited_for: The report supports recovered-plutonium fuel use and the intended benefits of more complete recycling.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate sustained recycling that consumes most long-lived actinides across the complete system.

sources.showed: This is a funding announcement for work intended to reduce the impact of used nuclear fuel.
sources.cited_for: The announcement supports funding interest in reducing the burden of used nuclear fuel.
sources.not_established: A funding announcement does not demonstrate repeated recycling or actinide consumption.

shown: Russia’s commercial BN-800 reactor has operated fully loaded with fuel containing plutonium recovered from spent fuel. This demonstrates reuse of recovered plutonium. Sustained recycling that also consumes other long-lived actinides remains a development goal.
missing: An integrated system would need to sustain recovery, fuel making and reactor use as the recycled material changes.
Measurements would need to establish net actinide destruction, including newly produced actinides and losses during processing.
Industrial operation would need to meet defined standards for cost, safety, reliability and controls against nuclear material diversion.
Every remaining waste stream would need measured quantities, suitable treatment and defined disposal requirements.

milestones.label: Commercial spent fuel completes repeated recycling and reactor use
milestones.explanation: Coordinated facilities would have to repeatedly recover material from commercial spent fuel, make usable fuel or targets, and return it to reactors while tracking every stream. This would demonstrate the complete recycling chain.

milestones.label: Measured destruction meets a predefined meaning of most
milestones.explanation: Inventories would have to track each isotope, a form of an element, including production, consumption, losses and uncertainty, against a predefined meaning of “most.” This would distinguish destruction from recovery or transfer.

milestones.label: Practical performance meets predefined thresholds
milestones.explanation: A demonstration would have to meet predefined thresholds for cost, exposures, releases, reliability, material controls, processing capacity and disposal needs against a comparison baseline. This would establish practical performance.

milestones.label: Independent checks confirm performance across repeated campaigns
milestones.explanation: Repeated campaigns would have to independently confirm performance across representative fuel variations within reported operating limits. This would establish how reliably the results persist and where they apply.

uncertain: Which actinides count, how much must be consumed, and over what period remain undefined.
The required processing capacity and acceptable practical performance thresholds remain undefined.
How much long-term disposal would remaining waste require after efficient actinide destruction?

page.title: Closed fuel cycle with minor-actinide transmutation
page.definition: A fuel cycle repeatedly recovers plutonium and minor actinides—neptunium, americium and curium—from used solid fuel, makes new fuel or targets, and returns them to fast-neutron systems for fission. Its complete material balance establishes net actinide destruction, including newly produced actinides and processing losses.

goal.need: On 25 August 2025, the IAEA reported that around 70% of spent fuel generated worldwide was in storage. The NEA's 2021 European accounting placed minor actinides with fission products in glass-bound waste after uranium and plutonium recovery. Recycling minor actinides addresses their contribution to waste heat and radiotoxicity.

completion.title: A licensed closed fuel cycle repeatedly recycles plutonium and minor actinides with net destruction.
completion.criterion: Operate an integrated, licensed fuel cycle that recovers plutonium, neptunium, americium and curium from used solid fuel, fabricates fuel or targets, irradiates them, and repeats recovery, fabrication and irradiation using the discharged material. Demonstrate net destruction by fission of recycled plutonium and minor actinides across the complete cycle, accounting for newly formed actinides, process losses, wastes and retained inventories. No common minimum annual throughput, operating duration or net destruction fraction is specified by the source bodies for this integrated test.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional integrated operational criterion.
completion.basis: Searched the IAEA's 2025 status report, NEA's TF-FCPT mandate, PATEROS, Euratom demonstration reports and NEWTON's funding opportunity for an integrated acceptance test specifying repeated actinide destruction, throughput and duration. They give objectives and component targets, but no such test. This provisional criterion combines their closed-cycle and transmutation objectives without assigning an unsupported destruction percentage.

milestones.title: A minor-actinide fuel is fabricated, irradiated and dissolved.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate fabrication, irradiation and dissolution of a candidate minor-actinide fuel, PATEROS's definition of technical feasibility. Critical fast reactors: a 2015 paper demonstrated laboratory electrorefining of irradiated METAPHIX-1 fuel containing 2 wt% minor actinides; its abstract gives no feed mass. Accelerator-driven systems: FAIRFUELS reported irradiation and examination of candidate fuels in Phénix during 2007–2009, without establishing their complete dissolution and recycle sequence.
milestones.set_by: Euratom PATEROS roadmap, section 6.5; the definition was originally stated for neptunium and americium in pressurised-water and fast reactors.
milestones.threshold_quote: ability of the fuel to be fabricated, irradiated and dissolved

milestones.title: A pilot plant can process the equivalent of 1 tonne of spent fuel for minor-actinide recovery.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate an Advanced Processing Pilot Unit capable of processing the equivalent of 1 tonne of irradiated fuel to supply minor actinides for demonstration irradiation. PATEROS specifies no annual throughput for this target. Both cases share this upstream separation requirement. ACSEPT's final report, updated on 4 June 2013, describes a hot GANEX test using 117 g of fast-reactor fuel; that experiment does not establish the 1-tonne capability.

milestones.title: A pilot plant has capacity to fabricate 100–200 kg of minor-actinide fuel per year.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate an Advanced Fuel Fabrication Pilot Unit with capacity of 100–200 kg of fuel per year, supplying prototype subassemblies and demonstration irradiation. Critical fast reactors: Rosatom reported three manufactured BN-800 trial assemblies on 22 April 2026, without an annual production rate. Accelerator-driven systems: a 2021 SCK CEN paper reports laboratory fabrication of ceramic-composite fuels. Neither source establishes this annual capacity; Rosatom's result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Euratom PATEROS roadmap, section 6.5; the target concerns solid transmutation fuels.

milestones.title: A fast-spectrum transmuter is available to irradiate minor-actinide fuel.
milestones.criterion: Make one or more fast-spectrum transmuters available for minor-actinide irradiation, PATEROS building block 3. Critical fast reactors: on 22 April 2026, Rosatom reported that three BN-800 assemblies containing americium-241 and neptunium-237 completed three fuel micro-campaigns; depletion measurements remained pending. Accelerator-driven systems: MYRRHA reported MINERVA building construction on 25 June 2026, without reporting reactor operation. Both reports are press releases, not peer-reviewed results.
milestones.set_by: Euratom PATEROS roadmap, building block 3, reproduced in the CDT final report.
milestones.threshold_quote: make available one or more transmuters

milestones.title: An engineering-scale plant reprocesses minor-actinide fuel and fabricates new fuel from it.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate an engineering-scale installation that processes discharged minor-actinide fuel and fabricates new transmuter fuel from the recovered material, PATEROS building block 4. Critical fast reactors: the 2015 METAPHIX-1 paper demonstrates laboratory actinide recovery from irradiated fuel, without pilot-scale refabrication. Accelerator-driven systems: no corresponding engineering-scale processing and refabrication result was located.
milestones.set_by: Euratom PATEROS roadmap, building block 4, reproduced in the CDT final report.
